own_scenes.desc: Primera encarnación de Jeff Mills (Detroit, 1963), que empezó a pinchar en sus dos últimos años de instituto, aprendió de los DJs de la Dale Willis Organization (con Ken Collier y Stacey Hale) y estudió unos años arquitectura. Deslumbró en Cheeks, en Eight Mile Road, y en el Nectarine Ballroom de Ann Arbor por la velocidad de sus manos. Jim Snowden, traído de la WBLS neoyorquina, lo fichó para competir con Mojo en WDRQ: como The Wizard nunca decía una palabra, con tres platos, cinta Otari y luego cuatro pistas, total libertad para interrumpir la programación y una actitud hip hop aplicada al electro, al new wave y al house. Para Claude Young, quien niegue su influencia en los ochenta miente.

refs.q: From these freedoms Mojo and I had, it created a lot of excitement because it gave impressions that radio was organic and free-flowing.
refs.para: When [Snowden] came to Detroit and WDRQ, he wanted very much to create a situation like NY Radio and was on the hunt to find a DJ from street. It was my position to compete with Mojo, so to give me complete and full freedom to play whatever was essential. To enhance this, I was given full access the record library WDRQ had and also a budget to purchase music. Later, I requested the authority to use the production studio and massive sound effects library. So, I could basically do anything and at almost anytime. There was a time that I could just abruptly interrupt normal programming and mix a few records just to keep people on the edge. It was really fantastic. From these freedoms Mojo and I had, it created a lot of excitement because it gave impressions that radio was organic and free-flowing.
refs.chapter: Cap. 3: Time to Express: Techno’s First Artists Emerge, 1981–1989

refs.q: Jeff took the hip-hop attitude to dance music, and as far as I know, no one else has approached it that way.”
refs.para: Mills’s mastery of multiple genres, thematic approaches, and technical precision have helped him rise to the very top of the DJ profession. Today, he is a respected techno artist and composer, yet still very much in demand as a DJ. Claude Young, who came up through the ranks much later and has recorded for Frictional, Seventh City Recordings, and the Belgian label Elypsia, has this to say of the man to whom he’s often compared: “Anybody who says that Jeff Mills was not an influence during that time period [the 1980s] is lying. Jeff took the hip-hop attitude to dance music, and as far as I know, no one else has approached it that way.”
